title: Research Bite #77: Exploring how understanding of the equals sign relates to additive and multiplicative equivalence performance beyond arithmetic fluency
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton breaks down a preregistered study by Phoebe Mills and colleagues that tested 277 pupils in their final year of primary school in Northern Ireland on what they think the equals sign means and how they handle equations where the answer does not sit immediately after it. The headline finding is a mismatch between recognition and understanding: almost every pupil could name the symbol, yet only about a fifth described it as showing that both sides hold the same value and none offered the substitution view. Calculation fluency explained most of the variance in performance, but the relational reading of the sign still predicted success on both additive and multiplicative equivalence once fluency and gender were controlled, and the effect was roughly twice as strong for multiplication. Barton converts this into classroom moves rather than leaving it as a research summary. He tells teachers to find out what pupils actually think the symbol means, to read equations aloud in the language of sameness, to move the equals sign around in practice sets, to extend the work to multiplication and division rather than stopping at addition, and to keep number fact practice running because fluency frees attention for structure. He is careful about the limits, noting that the design is correlational, the extra variance explained is one to two percent, and the sample is drawn from a single region.
points: Recognition of the symbol is near universal at 96.4 percent, while only 22 percent of pupils gave it a relational meaning and none offered the substitution view.
Calculation fluency explained over 70 percent of the differences in equivalence performance, so fact practice is not in competition with conceptual work.
The relational reading mattered about twice as much for multiplicative equivalence, which is precisely where classroom practice usually stops.
Most errors on two-sided equations came from calculating in the wrong direction, which makes mixed-format practice sets and public error discussion the obvious fix.
Barton flags the study as correlational with only one to two percent extra variance explained, so the classroom advice is offered as reasonable rather than proven.
quotes: This preregistered study looked at how 277 final-year primary pupils in Northern Ireland understand the equals sign, and whether that understanding matters once you account for how quickly and accurately they calculate.

Almost all pupils (96.4%) could name the symbol. Nearly half described it as a signal to work out an answer, 22% said it shows both sides have the same value, and none said the two sides could be swapped.

Most pupils leaving primary school still read the equals sign as “the answer comes next”. Those who understood it as meaning both sides have the same value did better on equations with the answer in an unexpected place, even after allowing for calculation skill.
This UK study shows the link holds for 11-year-olds even after accounting for calculation skill, and extends it to multiplication equations, where the connection was roughly twice as strong.
Say “three add four is the same as seven” or “has the same value as” rather than “makes” or “gives you”, and encourage pupils to use that phrasing when they explain their own working.
Calculation skill accounted for over 70% of the differences in how pupils did on these equations, far more than their understanding of the symbol.
The study is correlational and tested pupils once, so it can’t show that teaching the sameness meaning causes better performance.

These findings suggest that while arithmetic proficiency is important for success on equivalence problems, knowledge of the relational meaning of the equals sign also plays a role, particularly in more complex equivalence contexts.
